summary:
LuniX is an interactive web tool that lets mission planners, educators and
the public quickly and intuitively compare lunar landing sites and dates.
At the lunar poles, a site's solar power and direct Earth communications
depend on local terrain: a single ridge can cast a shadow for days. LuniX
covers the whole Moon with a clickable hexagonal grid on a real 3D globe
textured with NASA LOLA data. For any cell and any date, it computes
sunlight, solar power potential and Earth visibility over 30 days, using
horizon masks calculated from real LOLA digital elevation models and
precise Sun/Earth ephemerides. A threshold filter dims invalid zones, two
sites can be compared at two different dates, and a horizon view shows the
actual skyline from any site. A simplified public mode makes it accessible
to non-experts. LuniX turns hours of expert analysis into a single click.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LuniX answers a simple question: where and when should we land on the Moon?

Users pick any point on a 3D lunar globe or a 2D map, choose a date, and

immediately see whether the site gets sunlight, how much solar power it can

produce, and whether it has a direct line of sight to Earth for

communications — over a 30-day window.

HOW IT WORKS

- The whole Moon is covered by a clickable hexagonal grid (2,252 cells,

refining down to 100 m near points of interest).

- For every cell, a 360° horizon mask is computed from NASA LOLA digital

elevation models (5 m/px at the south pole sites, 236 m/px globally): the

Sun or Earth is only visible when it rises above the local terrain.

- Sun and Earth positions come from the open-source astronomy-engine

ephemeris library, lunar eclipses included; results were cross-checked

against JPL Horizons.

- The globe is textured with LROC imagery blended with LOLA hillshades; the

2D map offers photo, altitude, Sun-accurate hillshade and slope views.

- A threshold filter dims every zone that does not meet four adjustable

criteria (solar panels, Earth visibility, Sun, both combined), so valid

landing zones stand out at a glance.

- Users can pin a site, freeze the time of each panel independently, and

compare two sites at two different dates. A measurement tool provides

distances, areas and perimeters. A horizon view shows the real skyline

from any site, with Sun and Earth trajectories.

- Two interfaces: a Pro mode for mission planners, and a simplified public

mode for educators and the general public. Every indicator states whether

it is computed from real LOLA data or illustrative.

WHY IT MATTERS

Existing tools (QuickMap, Moon Trek, JPL Horizons) provide the raw

information but require expert knowledge and hours of work. LuniX turns the

same analysis into a single click, making site-date trade-offs accessible

to mission planners, educators and the public — the exact audience of the

challenge. The interface is bilingual (English/French) and runs offline in

any browser, with no installation.

TOOLS

JavaScript (Three.js for 3D rendering, astronomy-engine for ephemerides),

Python (rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow) for DEM processing, horizon mask

computation and texture generation. No server, no installation: the app

runs offline in a browser.

USE OF SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI)

All ideas, features and design decisions came from the team — AI did not

contribute to ideation. We used AI coding assistants (Claude, Mistral)

solely as programming tools, to write and debug the code implementing our

ideas, and to help draft documentation. Data validation (automated tests,

comparison with JPL Horizons) was done by the team. No SI-generated images,

audio or video are used in the project; all textures derive from NASA data

through deterministic scripts.
